meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't limit a child to your own learning, for he was born in another time'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Tagore. It's an anonymous proverb — documented from 1877 as an Arabic saying and later as Rabbinic — the Tagore credit is a post-2008 internet error.

answer.label: Not Rabindranath Tagore — an anonymous proverb
answer.sourceLine: According to Quote Investigator ↗, this saying is an anonymous proverb — its earliest known form appears in 1877 as an Arabic proverb, and it later circulated as a Rabbinic / Talmudic saying. The exact modern wording surfaced in a 1972 Jewish-quotations anthology. The credit to Rabindranath Tagore has no substantive evidence behind it and first appears only around 2008.

source.excerpt: Do not confine your children to your own learning, for they were born in another time.
trail: 1877 — earliest match. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the saying in Gems of the Orient (comp. Rev. A. Huebsch) as an Arabic proverb: “Do not confine your children to your own learning…”

1900–1972 — a Jewish / Rabbinic saying. Per QI ↗, it recurs in Talmudic and Jewish quotation collections; the exact modern wording appears in the 1972 Leo Rosten’s Treasury of Jewish Quotations, credited as Rabbinic.
c. 2008 — the Tagore error. QI ↗ finds no substantive evidence for Tagore and dates the first such ascription to around 2008 — possibly a slip from “Rabbinical” to “Rabindranath.”
Today — pinned on Tagore everywhere. Sites such as Goodreads ↗ present it as Tagore (often with “she”), with no source cited.
source.excerptNote: The 1877 Arabic-proverb wording. The now-popular “Don’t limit a child to your own learning, for he was born in another time” is a later rendering documented in a 1972 anthology.

source.rightsNote: The underlying proverb is old and anonymous (documented 1877), but the specific popular English wording is a later, un-authored rendering that surfaced in a 1972 anthology. Because no identifiable author or fixed first-publication can be tied to this exact wording, no public-domain claim can be made responsibly; the status is best treated as uncertain.

author.name: Anonymous (Arabic & Rabbinic proverb tradition)
author.heading: About Anonymous (Arabic & Rabbinic proverb tradition)
author.metaLine: Documented from 1877 · variously labelled an Arabic proverb, a Talmudic saying, and a Rabbinic saying
author.bio: This line has no known individual author. Reverend A. Huebsch’s 1877 anthology Gems of the Orient printed it among “Arabic Proverbs and Sentences,” and over the following century it reappeared in Jewish and Talmudic quotation collections, credited to no one. As Quote Investigator ↗ notes, someone may simply have confused “Rabbinical” with “Rabindranath,” handing the proverb to Tagore by accident.

misattribution.heading: How Tagore got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet-name” misattribution: an old, un-authored proverb re-pinned onto a famous, quotable figure.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence supporting the attribution to Rabindranath Tagore,” with the earliest such credit appearing only around 2008 — decades after the saying was already in print as a proverb.

Because the saying was widely labelled a Rabbinical saying (e.g. the 1972 Leo Rosten’s Treasury of Jewish Quotations), QI ↗ suggests an inattentive reader may have confused “Rabbinical” with “Rabindranath.”
Its earliest form (1877) sits among Arabic Proverbs; later collections call it Talmudic, Rabbinic, or a Hebrew proverb — never Tagore, per QI’s chronology ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest credit is anonymous — an old proverb of Arabic and Rabbinic pedigree, documented from 1877 and only mislabelled as Tagore after 2008 (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it feels like Tagore
lead: The sentiment — that each generation belongs to its own age and shouldn’t be bound by its parents’ knowledge — fits the humane, forward-looking Tagore of popular imagination, which is exactly why the misattribution sticks.
But the line predates any Tagore connection by over a century and was never sourced to him. Its real home is the anonymous proverb tradition, where wisdom travels without an author’s name attached.
context.pull: An old proverb wearing a famous name.
